0: When a general model cannot directly meet a specific business need, you can fine-tune it with your own business data so it learns the particular task and output style.
1: Take e-commerce entity recognition: we need the model to find product names, brand names and model numbers in the text and give their category and position. The model may chat about such products fluently, but in real use no required field may be missed, the fields must be consistent and the output format must be stable.
2: If the task and output requirements are clear and you have prepared examples, you can try fine-tuning on that data so the model learns the work you want done. Whether to update all parameters, and whether your GPU can cope, depends on the task and the resources.
3: Below, using ms-swift, we start from one LoRA fine-tune and run through data preparation, training, weight merging and inference in turn.
5: A general large model already has strong language understanding, knowledge Q&A and text generation. But in real business its performance may not directly meet a specific need.
6: For example, we may want the model to complete a certain information-extraction task accurately and output results in a prescribed format, or answer specific questions in a uniform way. For such needs you can train the existing model on specific data so it learns the task requirements and answering style. That process is called fine-tuning.
7: Fine-tuning is not training a model from scratch; it further adjusts a model that already has abilities, making it better suited to a concrete application. Compared with training a large model from scratch, fine-tuning usually needs less data and compute.
8: Today the common approach for fine-tuning large models is SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning). SFT trains the model on data with reference answers; each training record usually has an input and the corresponding output, so the model learns what to produce for a given input. In an information-extraction task, for example, a passage of text is the input and the correct extracted fields are the output. SFT suits tasks where clear training samples can be prepared, such as text classification, information extraction, question answering and fixed-format generation.
9: Besides SFT, large-model training can also use reinforcement learning (RL). Unlike SFT, which supplies reference answers directly, RL evaluates the quality of the model's output through reward signals and keeps adjusting the model's behaviour according to those rewards. Both SFT and RL belong to the post-training stage. Post-training is the series of training steps after large-scale pre-training that further improve instruction following, reasoning and specific task abilities. Large-model training usually starts with SFT to learn how to complete tasks following instructions, then combines methods such as reinforcement learning to further improve answer quality and behaviour.
11: Depending on the training method and hardware, you can choose LoRA, QLoRA or full-parameter fine-tuning. They differ in the number of trainable parameters, VRAM use and compute cost.
12: 1. Full fine-tuning (Full Fine-Tuning): during training all the model's parameters are updated, so the model can be adjusted fairly thoroughly. It also needs markedly more VRAM and compute, and training costs more.
13: 2. LoRA fine-tuning (Low-Rank Adaptation): to lower the hardware demands of fine-tuning, LoRA's core idea is to freeze the pre-trained model's weights and inject trainable rank-decomposition matrices into every layer of the Transformer architecture, greatly reducing the number of trainable parameters for the downstream task. During training only the original model's parameters are fixed and the down-projection matrix A and up-projection matrix B are trained. The LoRA diagram is shown in the figure.
14: Concretely, suppose the pre-trained matrix is \(W_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}\), its update can be written as:
15: \(W = W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA \)
16: Where \(\Delta W\) is the weight change to be learned during fine-tuning, \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}, \quad A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}, \quad r \ll \min(d,k) \), and A and B are the new parameters LoRA adds and trains. When training finishes you get a separate LoRA Adapter file holding the parameters from this fine-tune. To use it, load the base model together with the corresponding Adapter.
17: 3. QLoRA fine-tuning (Quantized LoRA): LoRA mainly reduces the resource cost of the trainable parameters, but the base model still has to be loaded into VRAM. If the model is large, loading the base model can still take a lot of VRAM. To lower the demand further you can use QLoRA.
18: The architecture is shown in the figure; QLoRA improves on LoRA mainly by using 4-bit precision together with paged optimisation to reduce the model's VRAM consumption.
19: QLoRA can be understood simply as quantization combined with LoRA. It quantizes the base model to lower precision; its main innovations are:
20: 1) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a new data type that is information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights;
21: 2) Double quantization, which reduces average memory use by quantizing the already-quantized constants;
22: 3) Paged optimizers, which help manage memory spikes and prevent out-of-memory errors during gradient checkpointing.
24: Choosing a fine-tuning method mainly means weighing model size, task needs, GPU resources and training cost. Each method has its scenario, and updating more parameters does not necessarily mean a better result. For most fine-tuning tasks, try LoRA first. LoRA trains only a small number of new parameters, needs relatively little GPU VRAM and compute, and the resulting Adapter file is small and easy to store.
25: If the base model is large and even loading it for LoRA leaves too little VRAM to train, consider QLoRA. QLoRA lowers the base model's own VRAM use through quantization, letting larger models be fine-tuned on limited GPU resources. QLoRA suits scenarios with a large model and limited GPU VRAM.
26: If GPU resources are plentiful and the task needs a more thorough adjustment, consider full fine-tuning. Because it updates all the model's parameters, it demands more VRAM, compute and training data, and training and saving the model cost more, so whether it is worth it usually has to be judged from the actual task.
27: In real projects we can validate the effect cheaply first, then decide whether to spend more on training. If LoRA already meets expectations there is usually no need to choose full fine-tuning just to update more parameters.
30: ms-swift (SWIFT, Scalable lightWeight Infrastructure for Fine-Tuning) is the open-source large-model training and deployment framework from the ModelScope community. Aimed mainly at large language models and multimodal large models, it offers a full set of tools from training and fine-tuning to inference, evaluation and deployment.
31: It already supports mainstream large language models such as Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama, GLM and InternLM, multimodal models such as Qwen-VL and InternVL, and the training of models or tasks such as Embedding, Reranker and text classification.
32: See ms-swift for more usage.
33: Besides training, ms-swift provides a fairly complete model workflow. After training you can run inference directly with swift infer, or deploy the model as an OpenAI-compatible API service with swift deploy. For inference and deployment you can also accelerate with engines such as vLLM, SGLang and LMDeploy.
34: For beginners, one feature of ms-swift is that it wraps up much of the complex configuration of large-model training. Specify the base model, training data, fine-tuning method and training parameters through command-line arguments and one fine-tune is done. In the experiment below we use ms-swift for a complete fine-tuning flow: preparing training data, launching LoRA training, reviewing the results, merging the LoRA weights, and loading the fine-tuned model for inference and deployment.
